idiom_name: module-scope functions plus class steps declared `private` or `#`
implementation_notes: As in JavaScript, the module is the practical privacy boundary, so the idiomatic composed method is an exported function or service method whose body lists small module-scope helpers; TypeScript adds two ways to state the boundary: the `private` modifier, checked by the compiler but erased at runtime (the handbook: 'private ... cannot be accessed from outside of its containing class'), and ECMAScript `#` private fields and methods (TS 3.8+, real runtime privacy), which are the right choice when a step must not be reachable at all. Prefer module-scope functions for stateless steps - they are tree-shakable and testable in isolation - and `private`/`#` class methods when the step reads `this` state. Keep the outline's types explicit so every step's contract is visible at the call site, and avoid `any` in step signatures, since it erases exactly the information the outline needs.
pitfalls: `private` is erased at runtime: the member is a normal property and `(order as any).step()` reaches it, so use `#step` whenever the boundary must actually hold rather than merely type-check.

Structural typing makes step signatures load-bearing: two steps whose parameters happen to have the same shape stay interchangeable even when they mean different things, so name and type each parameter as the step's contract.
A step passed as a callback loses its receiver unless it is an arrow function or bound; `noImplicitThis` catches some cases, and a detached helper that uses `this` still fails at runtime.
